summary:
Supply the length of the moving average and the price boxes (numbered 1 to 7) and the Moving average calculator solves for the answer. Think of it as a shortcut for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender.

The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Moving average calculator work?
sections.html:
The Moving average calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the length of the moving average and the price boxes (numbered 1 to 52).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: The formula behind the Moving average calculator
sections.html:
This one is not a single closed-form equation. It is driven by a page script that applies a set of rules — lookups, cut-offs and conditional branches — and the numbers you see are the script's output rather than the rearrangement of one line of algebra. The rules are what make the tool useful: a plain formula cannot express a table of thresholds or a choice between cases.

Practically, that means you can trust the result but cannot reproduce it with a pocket calculator. If you need to show your working, quote the inputs and the output rather than an equation.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Moving average calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the length of the moving average and the price boxes (numbered 1 to 7) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Moving average calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the length of the moving average and the price boxes (numbered 1 to 7), which is 55 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter price #1 in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Price #1 opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Moving average calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
